directions: Start tubers indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, or transplant seedlings after hardening off, into rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nonstop Mocca begonia is a compact series bred for reliable, continuous summer bloom in shaded containers and beds. Large, fully double, rose-like flowers in warm apricot-orange tones are held above deep bronze-black foliage, a striking dark-leaf selection within the popular Nonstop tuberous begonia series bred for compact size and near-continuous bloom from early summer through fall frost. Its shade tolerance and long, reliable bloom period make it a standout choice for a shaded container or bedding display where few other flowering plants perform as consistently in low light. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom, keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged, and in zones colder than 9, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after frost blackens the foliage.

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered, and transplant out after hardening off into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered, and transplant out after hardening off into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. This classic, widely grown seed series produces compact, uniform mounds smothered in flat, single flowers across a broad color range from white and pink to red, orange, and violet, long the standard bedding impatiens for shaded beds, window boxes, and mass plantings before disease pressure shifted many gardeners toward New Guinea impatiens hybrids. It flowers continuously without deadheading through a full shaded growing season, tolerating heat and humidity well, though it remains susceptible to impatiens downy mildew, a serious disease that has caused significant crop failures in some regions in recent years. Keep soil consistently moist, since impatiens wilt quickly in dry soil, and monitor closely for downy mildew symptoms (a white, fuzzy growth on leaf undersides) which can rapidly defoliate and kill plantings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; sky blue nemesia flowers best in cool weather and can stall or decline during peak summer heat.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; sky blue nemesia flowers best in cool weather and can stall or decline during peak summer heat. Delicate, fragrant, soft lavender-blue flowers cover a mounding, well-branched plant nearly continuously through cool spring and fall weather, providing a soft, cottage-garden color and light, sweet scent that many nemesia hybrids lack. Native to South Africa, it performs best in cool, mild climates or as a spring and fall bedding plant in hot-summer regions, where it may need to be replaced or given a summer rest during the most intense heat before resuming bloom as temperatures cool. Deadhead and shear lightly to encourage continued bloom, provide consistent moisture, and treat as a cool-season annual or short-lived perennial depending on climate.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained soil in full sun; twinspur flowers best in cool weather and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained soil in full sun; twinspur flowers best in cool weather and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Slender, wiry stems carry a profusion of small, coral-pink, spurred flowers over a long cool-season bloom period, more heat-tolerant and longer-lived as a perennial than many other diascia species and hybrids, native to South African mountain grasslands. It performs best in climates with mild summers or as a cool-season bedding plant further south, where the intense heat of a Gulf South or Deep South summer typically causes it to decline, making it better suited to spring and fall display than year-round performance in hot climates. Deadhead and shear lightly to encourage continued bloom, provide consistent moisture, and treat as a cool-season annual in hot-summer climates.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Wonder fan flower is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and blooms continuously through summer.

directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Wonder fan flower is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and blooms continuously through summer. Distinctive, one-sided, fan-shaped flowers in vivid violet-blue cover trailing stems nearly continuously from early summer through frost, needing no deadheading to maintain a nonstop flower display, making this a classic, reliable choice for a hanging basket or container that cascades attractively over an edge. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives through the hottest, most humid part of summer when many other trailing annuals decline, tolerating dry spells with minimal wilting. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and expect vigorous, trouble-free growth through the entire warm season without deadheading.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Blutopia bacopa flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and regular light feeding.

directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Blutopia bacopa flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and regular light feeding. Small, five-petaled, true-blue flowers smother trailing stems nearly continuously through the growing season, a rich, saturated blue less common among bedding annuals than the more familiar white bacopa cultivars, cascading gracefully over the edge of a hanging basket or container. Its trailing habit and reliable, continuous bloom make it a popular filler and spiller for mixed container arrangements, pairing well with upright, bold-flowered companions in a classic thriller-filler-spiller container design. Keep soil consistently moist, since bacopa wilts and drops flowers quickly if allowed to dry out, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain the heavy bloom display.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
